seeds.asked: 1) Regarding plasma proteins, explain site of formation {2 Marks}, mention six functions {6 Marks}.
seeds.label: The liver makes albumin, fibrinogen, the clotting factors and half the globulins while plasma cells make the gamma globulins, and between them the plasma proteins hold water in the capillary, buffer the blood, defend it, clot it, thicken it, seal the capillary pores, carry small molecules and store amino acids
seeds.definition: Plasma proteins are present at 7.2 to 7.4 g/dl and consist of albumin, globulins, fibrinogen and the other coagulation factors. The liver is the main site of synthesis, making albumin, fibrinogen, the coagulation factors and 50% of the globulins; the gamma globulins are made by plasma cells in lymphoid tissue. They contribute only 25 to 28 mmHg of the 5000 mmHg total plasma osmotic pressure, but the capillary wall is impermeable to them, so that small contribution is the effective colloidal osmotic pressure that draws tissue fluid back into the blood, and albumin dominates it because it is the most concentrated. They supply 15% of the buffering power of blood; the gamma globulins provide humoral immunity; fibrinogen and the clotting factors coagulate the blood; fibrinogen also contributes most to blood viscosity because of its elongated shape; plasma proteins close the pores of the capillary wall and so set capillary permeability; albumin and the alpha and beta globulins carry hormones, vitamins, lipids and minerals and stop them being lost in urine; and they are a reserve of amino acids for tissue protein.
seeds.objective: State where each class of plasma protein is formed and give six functions of the plasma proteins, naming which protein is responsible for each.
seeds.pitfall: Reading the small share of total osmotic pressure as a small effect. Crystalloids account for almost all of the 5000 mmHg, but they cross the capillary wall freely and so exert no net pull; the 25 to 28 mmHg of the proteins is the only part that acts across the capillary, which is why oedema follows hypoalbuminaemia.
seeds.subject: haem
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Plasma proteins

seeds.asked: 2) Compare between function of TXA2 and PGI2 {6 Marks}, and function of aspirin in preventing myocardial infarction {3 Marks}.
seeds.label: Thromboxane A2 from the platelet and prostacyclin from the endothelium are made by the same enzyme from the same substrate and do the opposite things, and that opposition is what keeps a platelet plug at the site of injury
seeds.definition: Thromboxane A2 is produced from arachidonic acid in the membrane of activated platelets by cyclooxygenase. It is a vasoconstrictor, a stimulator of the platelet release reaction and a powerful stimulant of platelet aggregation. Prostacyclin is produced from arachidonic acid in the endothelium of blood vessels by the same cyclooxygenase. It is a powerful vasodilator and an inhibitor of both platelet release and platelet aggregation. Because its actions are the opposite of those of thromboxane A2, prostacyclin keeps the platelet plug localised to the site of injury, and the balance between the two is one of the physiological limitations of blood coagulation.
seeds.objective: Compare thromboxane A2 and prostacyclin by their cell of origin and their three actions each, and explain what the balance between them achieves.
seeds.pitfall: Treating the two as products of different pathways because their effects are opposite. Both come from arachidonic acid through the same cyclooxygenase step; only the cell differs, and that is exactly why one drug acting on that step can shift the balance.
seeds.subject: haem
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Platelets and haemostasis

seeds.asked: 2) …and function of aspirin in preventing myocardial infarction {3 Marks}.
seeds.label: Aspirin prevents myocardial infarction because it inhibits cyclooxygenase in both cells but only the endothelial cell can make the enzyme again, so a small prolonged dose suppresses thromboxane A2 while prostacyclin recovers
seeds.definition: Aspirin inhibits the cyclooxygenase enzyme and therefore reduces production of both thromboxane A2 and prostacyclin. The endothelial cell produces new cyclooxygenase within a matter of hours, whereas the platelet cannot manufacture the enzyme at all. Administration of small amounts of aspirin for prolonged periods therefore reduces clot formation and has been of value in preventing myocardial infarction.
seeds.objective: Explain why inhibiting an enzyme common to both platelet and endothelium produces a net antithrombotic effect, and why the dose has to be small and prolonged.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming a bigger dose gives better protection. A larger dose suppresses endothelial prostacyclin as well, and the protective effect comes from the asymmetry between a cell that can replace the enzyme and one that cannot.
seeds.subject: pharm
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Platelets and haemostasis

seeds.asked: 3) Explain distribution and action of adrenergic receptors {9 Marks}.
seeds.label: Adrenergic receptors sit both on the effector organ and on the nerve ending that released the transmitter, and the two alpha and three beta subtypes are told apart by which second messenger they move and which plain muscle they act on
seeds.definition: There are two major types of adrenergic receptor, alpha with subtypes 1 and 2, and beta with subtypes 1, 2 and 3. Presynaptically they are autoreceptors on the membrane of postganglionic adrenergic nerve endings that regulate transmitter release: stimulating presynaptic alpha receptors decreases noradrenaline release and stimulating presynaptic beta receptors increases it. Postsynaptically, alpha-1 acts by raising intracellular calcium, alpha-2 by inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and lowering cAMP, and beta-1 and beta-2 by stimulating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP. Alpha-1 receptors are mainly excitatory and contract plain muscle: vasoconstriction in skin, viscera and male genitalia, the dilator pupillae producing mydriasis, the splenic capsule, the gastrointestinal sphincters retaining faeces, the internal urethral sphincter retaining urine, and the seminal vesicles and vas deferens in ejaculation. Alpha-2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax intestinal plain muscle. Beta-1 receptors are mainly excitatory and accelerate the heart and increase its force of contraction. Beta-2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax plain muscle: vasodilatation of coronary and skeletal-muscle vessels, bronchodilatation, and relaxation of gut, urinary bladder and uterus. Beta-3 receptors drive lipolysis.
seeds.objective: Give the presynaptic and postsynaptic distribution of adrenergic receptors, the second messenger each subtype uses, and the organ effect of each subtype.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming alpha always constricts and beta always dilates everywhere. Alpha-2 relaxes intestinal plain muscle and beta-1 excites the heart; the subtype, not the letter, decides whether the effect is excitatory or inhibitory.
seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Chemical transmission at autonomic junctions and autonomic receptors

seeds.asked: 4) In response to a systemic sympathetic response, epinephrine is released from the adrenal medulla. Which receptor does epinephrine bind to in cardiac muscle cells, bronchial smooth muscle cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells? A. β₁ | β₂ | α₂ B. β₂ | β₁ | α₁ C. α₁ | β₁ | α₂ D. β₁ | β₂ | α₂
seeds.label: Adrenergic receptors sit both on the effector organ and on the nerve ending that released the transmitter, and the two alpha and three beta subtypes are told apart by which second messenger they move and which plain muscle they act on
seeds.definition: There are two major types of adrenergic receptor, alpha with subtypes 1 and 2, and beta with subtypes 1, 2 and 3. Postsynaptically, alpha-1 acts by raising intracellular calcium, alpha-2 by inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and lowering cAMP, and beta-1 and beta-2 by stimulating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP. Alpha-1 receptors are mainly excitatory and contract plain muscle: vasoconstriction in skin, viscera and male genitalia, the dilator pupillae producing mydriasis, the splenic capsule, the gastrointestinal sphincters retaining faeces, the internal urethral sphincter retaining urine, and the seminal vesicles and vas deferens in ejaculation. Alpha-2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax intestinal plain muscle. Beta-1 receptors are mainly excitatory and accelerate the heart and increase its force of contraction. Beta-2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax plain muscle: vasodilatation of coronary and skeletal-muscle vessels, bronchodilatation, and relaxation of gut, urinary bladder and uterus. Beta-3 receptors drive lipolysis.

seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Chemical transmission at autonomic junctions and autonomic receptors

seeds.asked: 5) A 39-year-old woman returns home after eating at a buffet. An hour later she is relaxing in front of the television. Which of the following autonomic responses is most likely occurring at this time? A. Increased peristalsis. B. Increased sweating C. Decreased blood flow to the skin D. Dilation of bronchioles
seeds.label: The vagus carries the whole parasympathetic supply of the thoracic and abdominal viscera, slowing the atria, constricting bronchi, driving gut motility and secretion, and emptying the gall bladder
seeds.definition: Preganglionic fibres arise from the vagal nucleus in the medulla oblongata, run in the vagus to supply the entire thoracic and abdominal viscera — about 75% of all parasympathetic fibres — and relay in terminal ganglia in or close to the organ. On the heart the vagus does not supply the ventricles; it inhibits all properties of atrial muscle only, and decreases coronary blood flow and oxygen consumption. On the lungs it produces bronchoconstriction, dilatation of the pulmonary vessels and stimulation of the bronchial glands. On the gastrointestinal tract it contracts the plain muscle of oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and proximal large intestine, relaxes the sphincters, and is secretory to the gut glands, liver and pancreas. On the gall bladder it contracts the wall and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, evacuating it.
seeds.objective: Give the origin, course and relay of the vagal parasympathetic supply and state its effect on the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract and gall bladder.
seeds.pitfall: Saying the vagus slows the whole heart. It does not supply the ventricles at all — it inhibits the properties of atrial muscle only.
seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Parasympathetic nervous system

seeds.asked: 6) While driving, you narrowly avoid a car accident by slamming on the brakes. Your heart rate is accelerated (increased) when you come to a stop. Which of the following physiologic parameters will be decreased in response to this experience? A. Airway resistance B. Pupil dilatation C. Systolic blood pressure. D. Vascular resistance
seeds.label: The sympathetic system discharges as one unit in an emergency, and everything it does — dilating the pupil, accelerating the heart, constricting skin vessels, raising alertness, freeing glucose and fatty acids — is a preparation for flight, fear or fight
seeds.definition: The sympathetic nervous system is the catabolic, energy-consuming system, and in emergency it discharges as a single unit to prepare the individual for flight, fear or fight. It dilates the pupils, letting more light into the eyes. It accelerates the heartbeat and raises the blood pressure, giving better perfusion of vital organs and muscles. It constricts the blood vessels of the skin, which limits bleeding from wounds. It lowers the threshold in the reticular formation of the brain, reinforcing the alert and aroused state. It stimulates lipolysis and glycogenolysis, supplying more glucose and free fatty acids. In the lungs the same discharge produces bronchodilatation, so airway resistance falls while almost every other parameter rises.
seeds.objective: List the components of the sympathetic alarm response and say, for each, what advantage it gives in an emergency.
seeds.pitfall: Expecting every sympathetic effect to be an increase. Bronchodilatation lowers airway resistance and the gut wall relaxes — the discharge is uniform in purpose, not in direction.
seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Sympathetic nervous system

seeds.asked: 7) Adrenergic nerve fibers secrete: A. Acetyl choline B. Noradrenaline C. Dopamine D. Calcium ions
seeds.label: Autonomic fibres are named for the transmitter they release: cholinergic fibres are every preganglionic fibre, every postganglionic parasympathetic fibre and two sympathetic exceptions, and adrenergic fibres are all the remaining postganglionic sympathetic ones, which secrete noradrenaline
seeds.definition: Acetylcholine and noradrenaline are the main chemical transmitters at autonomic synaptic junctions, so autonomic nerve fibres are divided into cholinergic and adrenergic. Cholinergic fibres are all preganglionic autonomic fibres, sympathetic and parasympathetic alike including those to the adrenal medulla; all postganglionic parasympathetic fibres; and two groups of postganglionic sympathetic fibres, the secretory fibres to sweat glands and the vasodilator fibres to the blood vessels of skeletal muscle. All the other postganglionic sympathetic fibres are adrenergic and secrete noradrenaline, which is also secreted with adrenaline from the adrenal medulla. Cholinergic receptors are activated by acetylcholine and adrenergic receptors by noradrenaline.
seeds.objective: Say which autonomic fibres are cholinergic and which are adrenergic, and name the transmitter each releases.
seeds.pitfall: Calling every sympathetic postganglionic fibre adrenergic. The sudomotor fibres to sweat glands and the vasodilator fibres to skeletal-muscle vessels are sympathetic and cholinergic, which is why sweating is a sympathetic response blocked by an antimuscarinic.
seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Chemical transmission at autonomic junctions and autonomic receptors

seeds.asked: 8) Ciliary ganglion is considered as: A. Sympathetic collateral ganglion B. Parasympathetic terminal ganglion C. Parasympathetic collateral ganglion D. Sympathetic Terminal ganglion
seeds.label: There are four types of autonomic ganglion — the paravertebral sympathetic chain, the collateral ganglia, the terminal ganglia, and the adrenal medulla as a modified sympathetic ganglion
seeds.definition: The paravertebral sympathetic chain lies on both sides of the vertebral column with a ganglion for each spinal segment, except the cervical region, which has only three — superior, middle and inferior; it relays sympathetic fibres only. The collateral ganglia lie midway between cord and viscera at the origins of the large branches of the abdominal aorta and are named after them: coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric relay sympathetic fibres, while the ciliary, sphenopalatine, submaxillary and otic ganglia relay parasympathetic fibres. The terminal ganglia lie near or within the organ itself and relay parasympathetic fibres, whose postganglionic axons are only a millimetre to a few centimetres long. The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion whose postganglionic cells have lost their axons and secrete catecholamines into the blood.
seeds.objective: Name the four types of autonomic ganglion, give the site of each, and say which division of the autonomic nervous system relays there.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming every collateral ganglion is sympathetic because the abdominal ones are. The ciliary, sphenopalatine, submaxillary and otic ganglia are collateral ganglia that relay parasympathetic fibres.
seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Autonomic ganglia

seeds.asked: 9) Explain in biochemical basis: Mannitol has a clinical application {4 Marks}.
seeds.label: Mannitol is the sugar alcohol of mannose, and because the body neither absorbs it well nor metabolises it, it stays osmotically active in the fluid it is given into and is excreted unchanged by the kidney
seeds.definition: Sugar alcohols are sugars in which the carbonyl group has been reduced to an alcohol group; mannitol is the alcohol of mannose. It is poorly absorbed by the intestines, which is why it serves as a low-calorie sweetener. It is not metabolised in the body and is easily excreted by the kidney, so it remains osmotically active in the compartment it occupies. On that basis it is used as a diuretic, to reduce eye pressure in glaucoma and to reduce intracranial pressure in brain oedema, in each case by osmosis.
seeds.objective: Explain, from the fact that mannitol is neither metabolised nor reabsorbed, why it lowers intraocular and intracranial pressure and acts as a diuretic.
seeds.pitfall: Treating it as a drug with a receptor or a transporter to act on. Mannitol has no pharmacological target at all — the whole effect is the osmotic pull of a solute the body cannot dispose of.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Carbohydrates of Biological Importance

seeds.asked: 10) Explain in biochemical basis: Cholesterol is an important sterol and has many derivatives {4 Marks}.
seeds.label: Cholesterol matters because almost nothing else can be made without it — the bile acids, every steroid hormone and vitamin D3 all come from it, and it is the constituent that controls the fluidity of the cell membrane
seeds.definition: Cholesterol is the most important animal sterol; free cholesterol contains 27 carbon atoms and it circulates either free or esterified with a fatty acid. It is converted into bile acids and bile salts in the liver. It is the precursor of all the steroid hormones — the sex hormones and the corticoids. It is oxidised in the liver into 7-dehydrocholesterol, which ultraviolet light converts into vitamin D3 in the skin. And it is an important constituent of cell membranes, controlling their fluidity. It is excreted mainly in the bile as bile salts.
seeds.objective: Name the derivatives cholesterol gives rise to and state its structural role in the cell membrane.
seeds.pitfall: Filing cholesterol only as the substance that causes atherosclerosis. Every steroid hormone, both bile acid classes and vitamin D3 are built from it, and a cell that could not make it would have no membrane worth the name.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Lipids of Biological Importance

seeds.asked: 11) Explain in biochemical basis: Function of globin (protein) part of hemoglobin {4 Marks}.
seeds.label: The globin chain is what makes haem usable: it dissolves it, keeps its iron from being oxidised, keeps it inside the red cell, and tilts carbon monoxide away from the orientation it would otherwise prefer
seeds.definition: The globin part of haemoglobin has four functions. It makes haem soluble, because the polar amino acids of the folded chain lie on the surface. It prevents oxidation of haem into haematin, because the haem pocket is lined by nonpolar amino acids, and it also prevents formation of the haem-oxygen-haem complex. It prevents haem diffusing into the plasma, because of its large size. And it reduces the affinity of haem for carbon monoxide: isolated haem binds carbon monoxide with the iron, carbon and oxygen atoms perpendicular to the plane of the ring, but in haemoglobin the distal histidine sterically hinders that orientation, and binding at the less favoured angle weakens the haem-carbon monoxide bond.
seeds.objective: Give the four functions the globin chain performs for the haem group it carries, and the structural feature responsible for each.
seeds.pitfall: Thinking the globin merely carries the haem while the haem does all the work. Free haem is insoluble, oxidises to haematin, leaks out of the cell and binds carbon monoxide far more avidly — every one of those problems is solved by the protein around it.
seeds.subject: haem
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Hemoproteins

seeds.asked: 12) Explain in biochemical basis: Competitive inhibitors has an inhibitory functions on enzymes, explain how and enumerate 2 examples {4 Marks}.
seeds.label: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate closely enough to occupy the active site, so it raises the apparent Km without touching Vmax and is defeated by adding more substrate
seeds.definition: A competitive inhibitor is structurally similar to the substrate, so it competes with the substrate to bind reversibly at the active or catalytic site. The degree of inhibition depends on the ratio of inhibitor concentration to substrate concentration rather than on the absolute concentration of either, and on their relative affinities for the enzyme. Vmax is unaffected, because the inhibition is reversed by raising substrate concentration and at a high enough substrate concentration the reaction reaches the same Vmax as in the absence of inhibitor. The apparent Km rises, because more substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax. Examples are allopurinol, a structural analogue of hypoxanthine that inhibits xanthine oxidase and is used in gout; sulfonamides, structural analogues of para-aminobenzoic acid that block bacterial folate synthesis; and dicumarol and warfarin, structurally similar to a vitamin K derivative and used as anticoagulants.
seeds.objective: Explain how structural similarity to the substrate produces reversible inhibition, state what it does to Km and Vmax, and give two worked examples.
seeds.pitfall: Confusing it with allosteric inhibition because both are reversible. An allosteric inhibitor binds away from the catalytic site, changes the protein's conformation, and cannot be outcompeted by more substrate; a competitive inhibitor can.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Enzymes

seeds.asked: 13) Explain in biochemical basis: Collagen has a strong structure {4 Marks}.
seeds.label: Collagen is strong because every level of its structure is built for tightness — three residues per turn, glycine in every third position, a right-handed superhelix of left-handed chains, hydroxyproline hydrogen bonds, and covalent cross-links between chains
seeds.definition: The building unit of collagen is tropocollagen: three left-handed alpha-chains twisted into a right-handed superhelix, each chain about a thousand amino acids of the repeating triplet Gly-X-Y, where X is proline and Y hydroxyproline. Seven features give it its strength. Each turn contains only three amino acid residues, making a tight helix where an ordinary protein has 3.6. Glycine, in every third position, has a side chain short enough to let the chains lie very close together. The three left-handed chains form a right-handed superhelix. The high hydroxyproline content forms hydrogen bonds between chains. Covalent cross-links between adjacent chains give the tensile property, so collagen can be stretched without breaking. The molecules are arranged specifically into fibrils and then fibres. And the staggered, overhanging array gives collagen marked flexibility.
seeds.objective: Give the structural features, from the repeating triplet up to the fibre, that account for the tensile strength of collagen.
seeds.pitfall: Attributing the strength to proline alone. Proline prevents a right-handed helix from forming in the individual chain, but it is glycine at every third position that lets three chains pack close enough to wind together, and the covalent cross-links that let the result be pulled without breaking.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Proteins of Extracellular Matrix

seeds.asked: 14) Explain in biochemical basis: Non-sense and missense mutations can have severe effects, explain how and mention one example each {4 Marks}.
seeds.label: A base substitution in a coding region is nonsense if it creates a stop codon, missense if it changes the amino acid, and silent if the new codon is a synonym
seeds.definition: Base substitutions are the commonest gene mutations. A nonsense mutation converts an amino acid codon into a stop codon, so translation terminates prematurely and the protein product is usually non-functional — thalassaemia is the example. A missense mutation changes the codon so a different amino acid is inserted; the effect ranges from none to very serious, as in sickle cell anaemia, where glutamate is replaced by valine at position six of the β chain. A silent mutation gives a synonym codon for the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged.
seeds.objective: Name the three types of point mutation in a coding region and explain how each affects the protein product.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming every missense mutation is harmless because only one amino acid changes. Whether it matters depends on which amino acid — swapping polar glutamate for nonpolar valine creates the sticky patch that produces sickle cell anaemia.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Protein Synthesis (Translation)

seeds.asked: 15) Complete from the following words: {1 Mark each}. [ Serine - Alanine - Decreased - Tryptophan - Isoleucine - Not changed - Methionine - Increased ] - An example of a sulfur containing amino acid is a)………… and a one of a hydroxyl containing amino acid is b)…………. . - In protein denaturation, viscosity is c)…………. , and solubility is d)…………….. .
seeds.label: An amino acid is placed by holding two classifications at once — its chemical group and whether the body can make it — and no acidic amino acid is essential
seeds.definition: Chemically, glycine is the smallest neutral aliphatic amino acid, lysine is basic aliphatic, cystine is the disulfide-linked dimer of the sulfur-containing cysteine, isoleucine is branched-chain, and glutamate is acidic aliphatic. Nutritionally, the nine essential amino acids are valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, lysine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and histidine; arginine is half-essential; all the rest, including glycine, cysteine and cystine, and glutamate, are non-essential.
seeds.objective: Classify a named amino acid simultaneously by its chemical group and by whether it is essential in the diet.
seeds.pitfall: Calling cystine essential because methionine, the other sulfur-containing amino acid, is. Methionine is the essential one; cysteine and its dimer cystine are made in the body. There is no essential acidic amino acid at all.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Amino Acids of Biological Importance

seeds.asked: 15) Complete from the following words: {1 Mark each}. […] - In protein denaturation, viscosity is c)…………. , and solubility is d)…………….. .
seeds.label: Denaturation ruptures the bonds holding secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, leaving the primary sequence intact but the protein insoluble, more viscous, more digestible and biologically dead
seeds.definition: Denaturation breaks the bonds that stabilise the secondary, tertiary and quaternary orders, leaving only the primary structure. The protein loses solubility as its nonpolar groups become exposed, viscosity rises, digestibility by proteolytic enzymes rises because peptide bonds are exposed, biological activity is lost, and antigenic property is lost.
seeds.objective: List the effects of denaturation on a protein and say which level of structure survives it.
seeds.pitfall: Saying the peptide bonds are broken. Denaturation leaves the primary structure untouched — that is why a denatured protein is more digestible rather than already digested.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Proteins of Biological Importance

seeds.asked: 16) Complete from the following words: {1 Mark each}. [ Parallel - Hydrogen - Antiparallel - Fatherly - Covalent - Maternally - Circular - Linear ] - The 2 DNA strands run a)…………. and are joined by b)……..…… bonds. - Mitochondrial DNA is c)…….…… in shape and d)………….. inherited.
seeds.label: The two strands of the DNA double helix run antiparallel and are held to each other only by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — two for A-T and three for G-C
seeds.definition: Watson and Crick's double helix is the common physiological form of DNA. The two strands run antiparallel, are paired to each other and coil around a common axis to form a right-handed helix. They are held together by complementary base pairing through specific hydrogen bonds: adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine through three. The base pairs inside the helix are stacked above each other by Van der Waals forces and hydrophobic interactions, which stabilise the helix, and the whole resembles a spiral staircase in which the base pairs are the steps and the sugar-phosphate backbones the handrails.
seeds.objective: State the orientation of the two DNA strands relative to each other and name the bond that holds them together, with the number of bonds in each base pair.
seeds.pitfall: Calling the bond between the two strands covalent because DNA is chemically stable. The phosphodiester bonds along each backbone are covalent; the two strands are held to each other only by hydrogen bonds, which is why heat alone separates them.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Nucleic Acids

seeds.asked: 16) Complete from the following words: {1 Mark each}. […] - Mitochondrial DNA is c)…….…… in shape and d)………….. inherited.
seeds.label: Mitochondrial DNA is a small double-stranded circular supercoil that codes for the machinery of oxidative phosphorylation and is inherited only from the mother, because the mitochondria come from the ovum
seeds.definition: DNA is mainly linear, but it is circular in mitochondria, in chloroplasts and in bacteria. Mitochondrial DNA is 0.3 to 1% of the total cellular DNA and human mitochondrial DNA is a small double-stranded circular supercoil. It controls the synthesis of 2 ribosomal RNAs, 22 transfer RNAs and 13 proteins, most of which are involved in oxidative phosphorylation — the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis. Because the mitochondria are provided by the ovum, mitochondrial DNA molecules are maternally inherited and are used to trace maternal lineage. Mutations of mitochondrial DNA are associated with certain types of myopathy.
seeds.objective: Give the shape, the coding content and the pattern of inheritance of mitochondrial DNA, and say what makes the inheritance maternal.
seeds.pitfall: Explaining maternal inheritance as an X-linked pattern. It has nothing to do with the sex chromosomes — the zygote receives its mitochondria from the ovum, so an affected father transmits nothing and an affected mother transmits to all her children.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Nucleic Acids

seeds.asked: 17) Match: 1 mRNA 2 CAAT box and GC box 3 Polyadenylation of mRNA at 3’ end 4 TATA box 5 TFIIH 6 Alternative splicing — Explains why the estimated number of proteins much exceeds the number of genes / Has helicase and kinase activity / Control how frequently this event occurs / Determines the half-life time of mRNA / Synthesized by RNA polymerase II / Defines where transcription is to start along the DNA
seeds.label: The two promoter boxes divide the work — TATA says where transcription starts and CAAT and GC say how often — while TFIIH opens the strands, polyadenylation sets how long the message lives, and alternative splicing decides how many proteins the gene yields
seeds.definition: RNA polymerase II synthesises messenger RNA, most small nuclear RNAs and micro RNAs. The eukaryotic promoter carries two basal expression elements: the TATA box, of sequence TATAAA and 20 to 30 base pairs upstream of the start site, which defines where transcription is to start along the DNA; and the CAAT box and GC box, 40 to 200 base pairs upstream, which define when transcription starts and so control how frequently the event occurs. TFIID binds the TATA box first and the other transcription factors and RNA polymerase II assemble on it to form the pre-initiation complex; TFIIH then separates the two DNA strands by its helicase activity and activates RNA polymerase II. After transcription, the primary transcript is capped at the 5' end, polyadenylated at the 3' end by poly(A) polymerase — and the length of the poly(A) tail determines the half-life of the mRNA — spliced, and edited. Alternative splicing splices the primary transcript of some genes differently to yield different proteins from one gene, which explains why the estimated number of proteins much exceeds the number of genes.
seeds.objective: Assign each promoter element, transcription factor and processing step to the specific job it does in the making of a mature messenger RNA.
seeds.pitfall: Reading the TATA box and the CAAT box as two names for the same thing because both are upstream promoter elements. TATA fixes the start point and CAAT and GC set the frequency; a mutation in one changes where transcription begins and in the other changes how much message is made.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > RNA Synthesis (Transcription)

seeds.asked: 18) Match: 1 3’-Phosphodenosine-5’-phosphosulfate (PAPS) 2 ATP 3 S-Adenosyl Methionine (SAM) 4 FAD 5 cGMP 6 Coenzyme A — Hydrogen carrier / Methyl donor / Second hormone messenger / Synthesis of sulfur-containing compounds / Acyl group carrier / Source of energy
seeds.label: Free nucleotides do six different jobs — carry energy, signal as second messengers, donate methyl and sulfate groups, carry hydrogen and carry acyl groups — and which one a nucleotide does is fixed by the group hung on it, not by its base
seeds.definition: Beyond being the building blocks of DNA and RNA, free nucleosides and nucleotides serve four families of function. Energy transduction: ATP is the source of energy for mechanical and chemical processes, its bonds between the alpha, beta and gamma phosphates being high-energy bonds, and GTP serves the same role in some pathways. Signalling second messengers: cAMP is formed from ATP by adenylyl cyclase, and cGMP from GTP by guanylyl cyclase, cGMP mediating the smooth-muscle relaxation produced by nitric oxide and other vasodilators. Activated precursors in biosynthesis: S-adenosyl methionine is the most important methyl donor in transmethylation reactions; 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate is used for the synthesis of sulfur-containing compounds such as sulfated glycosaminoglycans and sulfolipids; CDP-choline and UDP-sugars serve phospholipid and glycogen synthesis. Coenzyme components: NAD+, NADP+, FMN and FAD are hydrogen carriers, and coenzyme A is an acyl group carrier through its active thiol group.
seeds.objective: Match each free nucleotide or nucleotide derivative to its biochemical role.
seeds.pitfall: Sorting them by their base — reading everything adenine-containing as an energy carrier. PAPS, SAM, FAD, NAD+ and coenzyme A all carry adenine and none of them is an energy source; the group attached to the nucleotide is what determines the function.

seeds.asked: 19) Diagram (1) [Phospholipid bilayer]. 1) ....………….. 2) ....………….. 3) ....………….. a) Explain why (2) increases the membrane fluidity. b) Explain why (3) decreases the membrane fluidity.
seeds.label: Membrane fluidity is set by how closely the phospholipid tails can pack: a cis-double bond kinks the chain and keeps them apart, a saturated chain is straight and lets them pack, and cholesterol sits between them controlling the result
seeds.definition: Phospholipids are amphipathic, with non-polar fatty acid side chains and polar head groups, and they are the important constituents of the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane. Increasing the unsaturated fatty acid content at carbon 2 of the phospholipids increases membrane fluidity, because the kinks produced by the cis-double bonds prevent the phospholipids from packing closely together. Saturated fatty acid chains carry no such kink, so they lie straight and pack closely, and closer packing means lower fluidity. Cholesterol is an important constituent of cell membranes that controls their fluidity, and it sits among the phospholipids of the bilayer.
seeds.objective: Identify cholesterol and the saturated and unsaturated fatty acid chains on a bilayer diagram and explain, from chain shape and packing, why each raises or lowers fluidity.
seeds.pitfall: Treating the double bond itself as what loosens the membrane. It is the geometry it imposes — a cis-double bond bends the chain, and a bent chain cannot lie flat against its neighbours; a trans-double bond leaves the chain straight and does not have the same effect.

seeds.asked: 20) Diagram (2) [Elongation of DNA]. a) Name of (1) and mention its function. b) Name of (2) and mention its function. c) Name of (3): ……………….
seeds.label: A replication fork is made by two proteins working together — helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds to open the duplex, and single-strand binding proteins hold the separated strands apart and protect them
seeds.definition: Helicase enzyme molecules attach at each origin of replication and unwind the DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous base pairs, producing replication bubbles. Single strand binding (SSB) proteins then bind to the single strands of the unwound DNA and stabilise them; without SSB proteins the two strands would simply rewind, and the proteins also protect the single strand from nucleases that cleave single-stranded DNA. It is the action of helicase and SSB proteins together that creates the replication fork. Topoisomerases relieve the supercoils that unwinding generates ahead of the fork.
seeds.objective: Name the two proteins that open and hold open the parental duplex at a replication fork and state what each contributes.
seeds.pitfall: Expecting the strands to stay apart once helicase has passed. Complementary single strands re-anneal spontaneously; the SSB proteins are what keep the template available, which is why they are drawn coating the separated strands rather than sitting at the fork apex.

seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > DNA Synthesis (Replication) and Repair

seeds.asked: 20) Diagram (2) [Elongation of DNA]. b) Name of (2) and mention its function.
seeds.label: The five eukaryotic DNA polymerases divide the work of replication: α primes, β repairs, γ copies mitochondrial DNA, δ makes the lagging strand and ε makes the leading strand
seeds.definition: DNA polymerase α, as the α–primase complex, lays down the RNA primers and the short DNA attached to them. DNA polymerase β fills the gap in DNA repair. DNA polymerase γ synthesises mitochondrial DNA. DNA polymerase δ synthesises the lagging strand from many primers, discontinuously as Okazaki fragments. DNA polymerase ε synthesises the leading strand continuously from a single primer. Polymerases δ and ε also proofread by exonuclease activity.
seeds.objective: Name the five eukaryotic DNA polymerases and give the specific job each one does.
seeds.pitfall: Swapping δ and ε. Epsilon makes the leading strand and needs only one primer; delta makes the lagging strand and needs many.

P1.prompt: Regarding plasma proteins, explain the site of their formation {2 Marks} and mention six of their functions {6 Marks}.
expects: Site: the liver is the main site of synthesis of plasma proteins — albumin, fibrinogen, the coagulation factors and 50% of the globulins are formed there
Site: the gamma globulins are formed by plasma cells in the lymphoid tissue

Osmotic function: the capillary membrane is impermeable to plasma proteins, so the 25 to 28 mmHg they contribute is the effective colloidal osmotic pressure that draws tissue fluid into the blood; albumin is the main protein responsible because it is present in the greatest concentration

Buffer function: plasma proteins supply 15% of the buffering power of the blood; at pH 7.4 they are negatively charged and combine with bases, mainly NaHCO3, forming the proteinic acid–sodium proteinate buffer system
Defensive function: the gamma globulins defend the body against microorganisms and their toxins — humoral immunity
Blood clotting: fibrinogen and all the clotting factors present in plasma are responsible for blood coagulation

Blood viscosity: blood is three times and plasma 1.5 times as viscous as water; fibrinogen contributes more than the other proteins because of its elongated shape, and viscosity maintains normal arterial blood pressure
Capillary function: plasma proteins close the pores in the capillary wall and so maintain normal capillary permeability; deficiency of plasma proteins increases it
Transport and conservation: albumin and the alpha and beta globulins carry hormones, vitamins, lipids and minerals, and binding prevents their rapid loss in urine and provides a reservoir
Source of amino acids: plasma proteins allow rapid replacement of tissue protein when tissue protein is depleted

P2.prompt: Compare the functions of thromboxane A2 and prostacyclin {6 Marks}, and explain the function of aspirin in preventing myocardial infarction {3 Marks}.

parts.prompt: Compare between the function of TXA2 and PGI2. {6 Marks}
expects: Thromboxane A2 is produced from arachidonic acid in the membrane of active platelets by the cyclooxygenase enzyme
TXA2 is a vasoconstrictor
TXA2 is a stimulator of the platelet release reaction
TXA2 is a powerful stimulant of platelet aggregation
Prostacyclin is produced from arachidonic acid in the endothelium of blood vessels by the same cyclooxygenase enzyme
Prostacyclin is a powerful vasodilator
Prostacyclin is an inhibitor of the release of platelets
Prostacyclin is an inhibitor of the aggregation of platelets
Since its actions are opposite to those of TXA2, prostacyclin keeps the platelet plug localised to the site of injury

parts.prompt: Explain the function of aspirin in preventing myocardial infarction. {3 Marks}
expects: Aspirin inhibits the cyclooxygenase enzyme and so reduces production of both TXA2 and prostacyclin
The endothelial cells produce new cyclooxygenase in a matter of hours, whereas platelets cannot manufacture the enzyme
Administration of small amounts of aspirin for prolonged periods therefore reduces clot formation and has been of value in preventing myocardial infarction

P3.prompt: Explain the distribution and action of adrenergic receptors.
expects: There are two major types of adrenergic receptor: alpha, with subtypes α1 and α2, and beta, with subtypes β1, β2 and β3
They are present on the surface of effector organs (postsynaptic receptors) and on the membrane of postganglionic nerve endings (presynaptic receptors)

Presynaptic receptors are autoreceptors that regulate transmitter release: stimulating presynaptic alpha receptors decreases the release of noradrenaline, and stimulating presynaptic beta receptors increases it
Mechanism: α1 acts by increasing intracellular Ca++; α2 by inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and decreasing cAMP; β1 and β2 by stimulating adenylyl cyclase and increasing cAMP

α1 receptors are mainly excitatory and contract plain muscle: vasoconstriction of the vessels of skin, viscera and male genitalia; the dilator pupillae, giving mydriasis; the splenic capsule; the sphincters of the gastrointestinal tract, retaining faeces; the internal urethral sphincter, retaining urine; and the seminal vesicles and vas deferens, in ejaculation
α2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax the plain muscle of the intestine
β1 receptors are mainly excitatory: cardiac acceleration and increased force of contraction of the heart

β2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax plain muscle: vasodilatation of the coronary and skeletal-muscle vessels, bronchodilatation, and relaxation of the gastrointestinal tract, urinary bladder and uterus
β3 receptors produce lipolysis

Noradrenaline excites mainly alpha receptors and the beta receptors only slightly, while adrenaline excites both approximately equally — so adrenaline has the greater effect on cardiac activity and on metabolism, and noradrenaline raises arterial blood pressure more

P4.prompt: In response to a systemic sympathetic response, epinephrine is released from the adrenal medulla. Which receptor does epinephrine bind to in cardiac muscle cells, bronchial smooth muscle cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells? A. β1 | β2 | α2 · B. β2 | β1 | α1 · C. α1 | β1 | α2 · D. β1 | β2 | α2 (Options A and D as printed are identical — see the unsat entry for this scheme.)
expects: Cardiac muscle cells: β1 receptors — cardiac acceleration and increased force of contraction
Bronchial smooth muscle cells: β2 receptors — bronchodilatation

Vascular smooth muscle cells: α1 gives vasoconstriction of the vessels of skin, viscera and male genitalia, and β2 gives vasodilatation of the coronary and skeletal-muscle vessels; α2 only relaxes the plain muscle of the intestine

A and D are printed identically as β1, β2, α2, and no printed option pairs β1 and β2 with α1, so the intended key cannot be recovered from the paper; A and D are the only options correct on the first two columns
Adrenaline excites both alpha and beta receptors approximately equally, which is why a single systemic release acts at three different receptor subtypes at once

P5.prompt: A 39-year-old woman returns home after eating at a buffet. An hour later she is relaxing in front of the television. Which of the following autonomic responses is most likely occurring at this time? A. Increased peristalsis · B. Increased sweating · C. Decreased blood flow to the skin · D. Dilation of bronchioles
expects: A. Increased peristalsis
Resting and digesting is the parasympathetic state; the parasympathetic system is the anabolic, energy-preserving system of rest, digestion and reading

The vagus contracts the plain muscle of the wall of the oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and proximal large intestine, relaxes the sphincters, and is secretory to the gut glands, liver and pancreas
Increased sweating and decreased blood flow to the skin are sympathetic effects — sudomotor secretion and cutaneous vasoconstriction
Dilatation of the bronchioles is a sympathetic effect; the vagus produces bronchoconstriction

P6.prompt: While driving, you narrowly avoid a car accident by slamming on the brakes. Your heart rate is accelerated when you come to a stop. Which of the following physiologic parameters will be decreased in response to this experience? A. Airway resistance · B. Pupil dilatation · C. Systolic blood pressure · D. Vascular resistance
expects: A. Airway resistance
The near miss triggers the sympathetic alarm response, in which the system discharges as one unit to prepare for flight, fear or fight
Sympathetic stimulation of the lungs produces bronchodilatation, and a wider bronchiole offers less resistance to airflow — so airway resistance falls
Pupil dilatation increases: contraction of the dilator pupillae gives mydriasis, letting more light into the eyes
Systolic blood pressure increases: the heart accelerates and its force of contraction rises, giving better perfusion of vital organs and muscles
Vascular resistance increases: the cutaneous and visceral vessels constrict, which also limits bleeding from wounds

P7.prompt: Adrenergic nerve fibres secrete: A. Acetyl choline · B. Noradrenaline · C. Dopamine · D. Calcium ions
expects: B. Noradrenaline

Adrenergic fibres are so named because they secrete noradrenaline; all postganglionic sympathetic fibres do so except the secretory fibres to sweat glands and the vasodilator fibres to the vessels of skeletal muscle, which are cholinergic
Noradrenaline is also secreted from the adrenal medulla together with adrenaline
Acetylcholine is the transmitter of the cholinergic fibres: all preganglionic autonomic fibres, all postganglionic parasympathetic fibres, and those two groups of postganglionic sympathetic fibres

Dopamine is an intermediate in the synthesis of noradrenaline — tyrosine is hydroxylated to DOPA, DOPA decarboxylated to dopamine, and dopamine converted to noradrenaline in the granulated dark vesicles — not the transmitter released
Calcium ions cause the exocytosis of the transmitter vesicles; they are not the transmitter

P8.prompt: The ciliary ganglion is considered as: A. Sympathetic collateral ganglion · B. Parasympathetic terminal ganglion · C. Parasympathetic collateral ganglion · D. Sympathetic terminal ganglion
expects: C. Parasympathetic collateral ganglion

The collateral ganglia that relay parasympathetic fibres are the ciliary, sphenopalatine, submaxillary and otic ganglia; the coeliac, superior mesenteric, aorticorenal and inferior mesenteric relay sympathetic fibres

Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve arise in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and relay in the ciliary ganglion; the postganglionic fibres enter the eye as the short ciliary nerves
It is not a terminal ganglion: terminal ganglia lie near or within the visceral organ itself and their postganglionic fibres are only 1 mm to a few centimetres long
It is not sympathetic: the paravertebral chain relays sympathetic fibres only, and the abdominal collateral ganglia are the sympathetic collateral ones

B9.prompt: Explain, on a biochemical basis, why mannitol has a clinical application.
expects: Sugar alcohols are sugars in which the carbonyl group is reduced to an alcohol group; mannitol is mannose alcohol
It is poorly absorbed by the intestines, so it is used as a low-calorie sweetener
It is non-metabolised in the body and easily excreted by the kidney
Because it stays in the fluid it is given into and is excreted unchanged, it acts by osmosis
It is used as a diuretic, to reduce eye pressure in glaucoma, and to reduce intracranial pressure in brain oedema

B10.prompt: Explain, on a biochemical basis, why cholesterol is an important sterol with many derivatives.
expects: Cholesterol is the most important animal sterol; free cholesterol contains 27 carbon atoms and it is present either free or esterified with a fatty acid
It is converted into bile acids and bile salts in the liver
It is the precursor of all steroid hormones — the sex hormones and the corticoids
It is oxidised in the liver into 7-dehydrocholesterol, which is converted into vitamin D3 under the skin by ultraviolet rays
It is an important constituent of cell membranes and controls their fluidity
It is excreted from the body mainly in the bile in the form of bile salts

B11.prompt: Explain, on a biochemical basis, the function of the globin (protein) part of haemoglobin.
expects: It makes haem soluble, because of the polar amino acids on the surface of the folded chain
It prevents oxidation of haem into haematin, because the haem pocket is lined by nonpolar amino acids; it also prevents formation of the haem-O2-haem complex
It prevents diffusion of haem into the plasma, because of its large size

It reduces the affinity of haem for carbon monoxide: carbon monoxide binds isolated haem with the iron, carbon and oxygen atoms perpendicular to the plane of the haem, but in haemoglobin the distal histidine sterically hinders that orientation, and binding at the less favoured angle reduces the strength of the haem-CO bond

B12.prompt: Explain, on a biochemical basis, how competitive inhibitors inhibit enzymes, and enumerate two examples.
expects: A competitive inhibitor is structurally similar to the substrate, so it competes with the substrate to bind reversibly at the active (catalytic) site

The degree of inhibition depends on the ratio of the concentration of the inhibitor to that of the substrate, not on the absolute concentration of either, and on their relative affinities for the enzyme

There is no effect on Vmax: the inhibition is reversed by increasing the substrate concentration, and at a sufficiently high substrate concentration the reaction reaches the Vmax observed without inhibitor
The apparent Km increases: more substrate is needed to achieve half of Vmax
Example — allopurinol: a structural analogue of hypoxanthine that inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme forming uric acid from hypoxanthine, and is used in the treatment of gout
Example — sulfonamides: structural analogues of para-aminobenzoic acid that inhibit the bacterial enzyme forming folic acid from PABA, making them bacteriostatic
Example — dicumarol and warfarin: structurally similar to a vitamin K derivative required for the activation of clotting factors, and used as anticoagulants

B13.prompt: Explain, on a biochemical basis, why collagen has a strong structure. (The companion copy of this paper records the instruction as "mention 4 points".)
expects: Each turn contains three amino acid residues, making a tight helix, where normal proteins contain 3.6 amino acids per turn
The presence of glycine, with its short side chain, in every third position makes the polypeptide chains lie very close to each other
The three left-handed coiled peptide chains form a right-handed superhelix
The high content of hydroxyproline forms hydrogen bonds between the chains
Covalent cross-linkages between adjacent polypeptide chains are responsible for the tensile property of collagen — it can be stretched without being broken
The specific arrangement into fibrils and fibres
The staggered array (overhanging) gives marked flexibility to collagen

B14.prompt: Explain, on a biochemical basis, how nonsense and missense mutations can have severe effects, and mention one example of each.
expects: Nonsense mutation: an amino acid codon is converted into a stop (non-sense) codon
Translation of the mRNA from that gene is prematurely terminated, so the protein product is truncated and usually non-functional
Example of a nonsense mutation: thalassaemia — defective production of either the alpha chain or the beta chain of globin
Missense mutation: the codon is changed so that a different amino acid is inserted into the protein product, and the effect ranges from none to very serious depending on which amino acid is changed
Example of a missense mutation: sickle cell anaemia — a single nucleotide alteration in the beta-globin gene replaces polar glutamate at position six with nonpolar valine

That generates a hydrophobic sticky patch on the beta subunit, and at low pO2 deoxy-HbS polymerises into long insoluble fibres, producing rigid misshapen erythrocytes that block narrow capillaries and are removed early by the spleen
